notes:
Here are the verse‑by‑verse notes for Genesis 18, compiled from the traditional Protestant commentary sources I was able to access. Where denominational differences or other views were available in the sources, I have noted them.

---

## Genesis 18 – Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

### v. 1
- **“The LORD appeared to Abraham”**: This is a continuation of the circumcision narrative of Genesis 17 (Ellicott). It is the fifth or sixth recorded appearance of Yahweh to Abraham (Precept Austin counts five; Constable counts six). The time is shortly after Genesis 17 — no more than about three months later, since in Gen 17:21 God said Sarah would give birth in a year and here she is not yet pregnant (Guzik). [enduringword.com](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-18/)
- **Jewish tradition** adds that this visit happened on the third day after Abraham’s circumcision, for the purpose of healing him — explaining why he was resting at home instead of being in the field (Ellicott, citing rabbinic sources). [biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/18.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/18.htm)
- **“Oaks of Mamre”**: Hebrew is literally “oaks” or “terebinths” of Mamre (Pulpit, Ellicott, Precept Austin). This was Abraham’s long‑standing dwelling place (Gen 13:18; 14:13), near Hebron, about 19 miles southwest of Jerusalem. Trees in a semi‑arid climate signified the presence of water and provided crucial shade (Precept Austin). [preceptaustin.org/genesis-18-commentary](https://www.preceptaustin.org/genesis-18-commentary)
- **“Heat of the day”**: Noon, the time of rest and dinner in the ancient Near East (Pulpit). Abraham was likely sitting in the tent opening to catch any breeze (Ellicott). Courson (cited at Precept Austin) sees “the heat of the day” as a biblical picture of hard trials — times when the Lord often reveals Himself most clearly (cf. the fiery furnace in Daniel 3). [preceptaustin.org/genesis-18-commentary](https://www.preceptaustin.org/genesis-18-commentary)

### v. 2
- **“Three men”**: The chapter opens by saying “the LORD appeared,” so one of the three is clearly Yahweh in human form; the other two are angels (Gill, Guzik, Ellicott, Precept Austin), identified as such in Gen 19:1. The three are **not** manifestations of the three Persons of the Trinity (Pulpit explicitly rejects that view; Precept Austin notes that the Church of England reads Gen 18 on Trinity Sunday because of the three‑in‑one pattern, but cautions against using it as proof of the Trinity; Guzik holds this is a Christophany — a pre‑incarnate appearance of the Son). [enduringword.com](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-18/); [biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/18.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/18.htm)
- **“Ran… bowed himself to the ground”**: Abraham’s running was unusual for an elderly sheikh of high standing, suggesting he recognised these were no ordinary travellers (Precept Austin, Guzik). The Hebrew verb *shachah* (bow) is translated in the Septuagint as *proskuneo* — to prostrate in worship, not mere courtesy (Precept Austin). Gill thinks it was civil honour only, since Abraham did not yet know they were divine — though Gill allows that Abraham addressed the chief one as “My Lord” (Adonai). [preceptaustin.org/genesis-18-commentary](https://www.preceptaustin.org/genesis-18-commentary); [biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/18.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/18.htm)

### v. 3
- **“My lord” (Adonai)**: Ellicott says this is a term of simple respect, like “Sir,” used by an Arab sheikh to a passing traveller. Pulpit says the better reading is the singular “Adonai” (Lord) rather than “Adoni” (my lord), possibly indicating Abraham already sensed he was addressing deity. Gill similarly notes Abraham singled out the one who appeared greatest. Guzik holds that Abraham knew this was the Lord by spiritual intuition. [biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/18.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/18.htm); [enduringword.com](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-18/)

### v. 4–5
- **Hospitality customs**: Foot‑washing was the first necessity of Oriental hospitality — not only to clean dusty feet protected only by sandals, but to cool the whole body (Ellicott). “Rest yourselves under the tree” literally means “recline by resting on the elbow” (Pulpit). Abraham’s “morsel of bread” is typical Eastern understatement — what follows is a lavish feast (Pulpit, Ellicott). [biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/genesis/18.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/genesis/18.htm)
- **“For therefore are ye come”**: Abraham suggests his tent was pitched near the route precisely so he could exercise hospitality — a sacred duty of an Arab sheikh (Ellicott). Calvin saw it as God having providentially directed the travellers his way (Pulpit). [biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/18.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/18.htm)

### v. 6
- **“Three seahs of fine flour”**: A seah was about a third of an ephah — roughly a peck and a half in modern terms (Pulpit); three seahs made about a bushel of flour (Gill). This was an enormous quantity of bread. Guzik notes the meal would have taken considerable time to prepare, yet Abraham and Sarah did it themselves rather than delegating it all to servants. [enduringword.com](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-18/); [biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/18.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/18.htm)

### v. 7
- **“Tender and choice calf”**: Veal was a delicacy reserved for honoured guests; it was not part of the ordinary Bedouin meal (Ellicott). That Abraham selected and slaughtered it himself shows he regarded his visitors as persons of the highest rank (Ellicott, Guzik). The “young man” to whom he gave it is identified by one Jewish tradition as Ishmael (Gill, citing Jarchi). [biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/18.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/18.htm); [biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/18.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/18.htm)

### v. 8
- **“Curds and milk and the calf”**: “Butter” in older translations is better rendered “curds” or curdled milk (Ellicott). The Hebrews, Greeks, and Romans did not know how to make butter in the modern sense (Ellicott). This was a “stately repast” — bread, veal, fresh milk, and sour milk (Ellicott). [biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/18.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/18.htm)
- **“Stood by them… as they ate”**: Abraham, like an honoured host, stood and served rather than sitting with them. This was customary among great personages in the East (Gill, citing Shaw’s Travels). Jewish tradition (Targum of Jonathan) translates “they seemed to eat,” uneasy with the idea of angels eating; but the text plainly says they ate, and the NT shows the risen Christ eating (Luke 24:41‑43) — so eating by spiritual beings in bodily form is not impossible (Precept Austin / Bible.org). [preceptaustin.org/genesis-18-commentary](https://www.preceptaustin.org/genesis-18-commentary)

### v. 9–10
- **“Where is Sarah your wife?”**: The question was contrary to Oriental manners — women were not directly mentioned (Ellicott). It signals that the visit had special significance for Sarah (Garner‑Howes Baptist Commentary). The One speaking now is clearly the Lord (v. 10, 13 “the LORD said”). [biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/18.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/18.htm)
- **“At this time next year”**: Hebrew “according to the time of life” — Ellicott says the best rendering is “a year hence,” not “next spring.” The Targums and Jewish tradition take it as “at this time next year” and associate it with Passover. Gill notes it could mean the full nine‑month term of a living child. [biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/18.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/18.htm); [biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/18.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/18.htm)

### v. 11–12
- **“Sarah had passed the age of childbearing”**: literally “the manner of women had ceased to be with Sarah” — she had gone through menopause (Guzik, Gill). Even accounting for the long lifespans (Abraham 175, Sarah 127), both were well past middle age; the birth would require a miracle (Guzik). [enduringword.com](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-18/)
- **“Sarah laughed within herself”**: It was an inward, silent laugh — not audible, yet God heard it (Guzik). Her words “After I am worn out… shall I have pleasure?” refer to sexual pleasure in conceiving a child. Leupold (cited by Guzik) observes, “The matter is not put very delicately by Sarah.” The laughter was one of disbelief, not joy — the same reaction Abraham had in Gen 17:17 (Ellicott). Yet God did not withdraw the promise; He dealt with her unbelief (Guzik). [enduringword.com](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-18/)

### v. 13–14
- **“Why did Sarah laugh?”**: God addressed Abraham, not Sarah, because Abraham was the head of the home (Guzik). The question exposed Sarah’s secret unbelief and demonstrated divine omniscience — God hears even inward thoughts (Garner‑Howes). [enduringword.com](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-18/)
- **“Is anything too difficult for the LORD?”**: The Hebrew word for “hard/difficult” (*pālā’*) is the same word translated “Wonderful” in Isaiah 9:6 — pointing forward to Christ (Guzik). John Piper (Desiring God / Reformed Baptist) emphasises that this question is “the great missionary question”: God waited until the situation was humanly impossible — Sarah barren all her life and now post‑menopausal — specifically to demonstrate that nothing is too hard for Him, and that the covenant people are created by sovereign grace, not human effort. [desiringgod.org/messages/is-anything-too-hard-for-god](https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/is-anything-too-hard-for-god); [enduringword.com](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-18/)

### v. 15
- **“Sarah denied it… for she was afraid”**: Ellicott calls this “the inconsistency of fright” — she now knew the speaker was divine and that He perceived her secret thoughts, yet she took refuge in falsehood. The gentle rebuke “No, but you did laugh” was aimed at building her faith, just as the angel’s words later built Mary’s faith (Luke 1:34‑37). Guzik notes God never withdrew the promise despite her weak faith — “If we are faithless, He remains faithful” (2 Tim 2:13). [biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/18.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/18.htm); [enduringword.com](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-18/)

### v. 16
- **“The men got up… looked toward Sodom”**: The three “men” — the Lord and two angels — set their faces toward Sodom. Abraham, in customary Eastern fashion, accompanied his departing guests for part of their journey (Ellicott, Guzik). The route would have been southeast over the hill‑country of Judah; tradition says Abraham went with them as far as Caphar‑Barucha, from which the Dead Sea is visible through a deep ravine (Ellicott). [biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/18.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/18.htm)

### v. 17–19
- **“Shall I hide from Abraham what I am about to do?”**: God asked this question not because He needed counsel but to reveal His thinking to the reader (Guzik). The reason given (vv. 18‑19) is twofold: (1) Abraham will become a great and mighty nation through whom all nations will be blessed; (2) God has “chosen” (or “known”) him so that he would command his household to keep the way of the LORD in righteousness and justice (Guzik, Ellicott). [enduringword.com](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-18/)
- **“I have chosen him”** (BSB) / **“I have known him”** (KJV): Ellicott says the Hebrew means “I have known him *in order that* he may command his sons…” — emphasising the **purpose** of God’s electing knowledge: that Abraham would lead his household in covenant faithfulness. The Garner‑Howes Baptist Commentary stresses that this establishes the father (not the state, church, or school) as the divinely appointed teacher of children in spiritual and moral matters. [biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/18.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/18.htm); [studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/genesis-18.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/genesis-18.html)

### v. 20–21
- **“The outcry against Sodom and Gomorrah is great”**: The “outcry” came from multiple sources — God’s own justice, the victims of the cities’ depravity, even creation itself (Guzik). Their sin is described as “very grave” — literally “abundant and heinous” (Garner‑Howes). Guzik lists the sources of the outcry: (1) God and His holy justice, (2) onlooking angelic beings, (3) the multitude of victims, (4) creation itself affected by unnatural transgression. [enduringword.com](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-18/)
- **“I will go down… to see”**: This is anthropomorphic language. God did not need to “go down” to find out — He already knew. The statement demonstrates to us the thorough character of God’s knowledge and the integrity of His justice (Guzik, Ellicott). Ellicott adds that the two angels went to Sodom to give the people a final trial: “If they meet with upright treatment, then God will know that there are limits to the wickedness of its inhabitants.” [enduringword.com](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-18/); [biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/18.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/18.htm)

### v. 22
- **“The two men turned… toward Sodom, but Abraham remained standing before the LORD”**: The two angels departed (cf. Gen 19:1), while the third — Yahweh Himself — remained with Abraham (Guzik, Ellicott, Precept Austin). This verse marks the beginning of the first extended intercessory prayer recorded in Scripture (Preacher’s Complete Homiletical Commentary). Abraham now stands before God with a specific plea. [enduringword.com](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-18/); [preceptaustin.org/genesis-18-commentary](https://www.preceptaustin.org/genesis-18-commentary)

### v. 23–25
- **“Will You really sweep away the righteous with the wicked?”**: Abraham’s intercession is “unspeakably noble” (Ellicott). He begins by establishing a principle — that the Judge of all the earth must do what is right. He was not thinking only of Lot; he had seen the human affection of the people of Sodom when he rescued them (Gen 14) and hoped some had repented (Ellicott). The Hebrew verb “sweep away” (*sāpâ*) suggests indiscriminate ruin (Ellicott). [biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/18.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/18.htm)
- **“Far be it from You!”**: Abraham “reminded the Lord of His own nature” (Guzik). Effective intercession knows who God is and prays according to His revealed character. Guzik notes that Abraham’s compassion extended even to the notoriously wicked — he did not simply pray “get Lot out,” but interceded for the whole city. [enduringword.com](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-18/)

### v. 26
- **“If I find fifty righteous… I will spare the whole place”**: God immediately granted Abraham’s request. Ellicott says Abraham did not begin at fifty as a negotiating tactic, but because the readiness with which each prayer was heard emboldened him to press further. God’s gracious response illustrates 2 Peter 3:9 — He desires that none should perish. [biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/18.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/18.htm)

### v. 27
- **“I am but dust and ashes”**: An expression of profound humility. Abraham contrasts his mortal frailty with the majesty of the Lord he addresses. His boldness in intercession is matched by his self‑abasement (Guzik). [enduringword.com](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-18/)

### v. 28–32
- **The negotiation (45, 40, 30, 20, 10)**: Abraham reduced the number in two stages — first by fives (50 → 45), then by tens (40 → 30 → 20 → 10). Guzik calls this “bold humility” and notes that Abraham’s intercession was **specific** — he negotiated actual numbers, not vague generalities. “Prayers are often ineffective because believers really don’t ask the Lord to do anything.” His persistence models the truth that an intercessor must sometimes feel that eternal destinies depend on his prayer. [enduringword.com](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-18/)
- **“May the Lord not be angry”**: This phrase is repeated (vv. 30, 32), showing Abraham’s awareness that he was pressing the limits of boldness. Yet he continued — not from pride, but from a heart of love (Guzik). [enduringword.com](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-18/)
- **Why stop at ten?** Guzik speculates that Abraham may have thought Lot would surely have won at least six converts beyond his own family (Lot, his wife, two daughters, and perhaps sons‑in‑law). Only four were actually righteous in the city. Ellicott says Abraham ended his entreaty because he had obtained all he asked for; the purpose of the revelation was fulfilled. [enduringword.com](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-18/); [biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/18.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/18.htm)

### v. 33
- **“The LORD departed… Abraham returned home”**: Ellicott says God did not depart to avoid further importunity — Abraham had already obtained all he asked. The purpose of the whole revelation was fulfilled: it showed that the Gentile world was subject to Jehovah’s dominion and that there was mercy for it as well as for the covenant people — a lesson later echoed in the Book of Jonah (Ellicott). Guzik reflects that even though Sodom was ultimately destroyed (because there were not even ten righteous), the intercession was not in vain: God specifically revealed the fate of the city to draw out of Abraham “an intercessor’s heart of love,” conforming him to the image of Christ, the great Intercessor (Heb 7:25). [biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/18.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/18.htm); [enduringword.com](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-18/)

---

## Where Protestant Traditions Differ

From the sources accessed, the main differences centre on **v. 2** (the identity of the “three men”) and **v. 3** (whether Abraham recognised them as divine):

- **Pentecostal/Charismatic (Enduring Word / David Guzik)**: Strongly holds that this is a pre‑incarnate appearance of Jesus Christ (a Christophany), since no one has seen God the Father (John 1:18; 1 Tim 6:16). Abraham recognised the Lord and worshipped. The chapter models bold, specific, persistent intercessory prayer. [enduringword.com](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-18/)

- **Reformed Baptist (John Piper / Desiring God)**: Focuses on v. 14 — “Is anything too hard for the LORD?” — as the key missionary and theological question. God deliberately waited until it was humanly impossible for Sarah to conceive so that the covenant people would be seen as a work of sovereign grace, not human effort (the “Isaac Factor”). [desiringgod.org/messages/is-anything-too-hard-for-god](https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/is-anything-too-hard-for-god)

- **Older Baptist (Gill)**: Holds that Abraham initially treated the three as human travellers and bowed in civil courtesy only; he addressed the chief one as “my Lord” in the sense of “Sir.” One of the three was the Son of God in human form, the other two were created angels. Gill explicitly rejects the view that all three were the Trinity. [biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/18.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/18.htm)

- **Anglican (Ellicott)**: The number three “pointed also to the Trinity,” which is why the Church of England reads this as a lesson for Trinity Sunday. But Ellicott cautions against using it as a proof‑text for the doctrine, lest it imply a personal appearance of the Father and Spirit, “which would savour of heretical impiety.” Ellicott holds that Abraham addressed the visitors with ordinary Oriental courtesy and only later realised their divine identity. [biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/18.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/18.htm)

- **Evangelical (Precept Austin / multiple teachers)**: Generally aligns with the Christophany view, but also notes the Church of England’s Trinitarian reading as a secondary application. Precept Austin cites Skip Heitzig emphasising that God works “by invitation” — He waited for Abraham to invite Him in — and Jon Courson noting that the 99‑year‑old Abraham “ran” to meet the Lord as a model of eager devotion. [preceptaustin.org/genesis-18-commentary](https://www.preceptaustin.org/genesis-18-commentary)

- **Baptist (Garner‑Howes / StudyLight)**: Emphasises the father’s role as the divinely appointed teacher (v. 19 — “he will command his children and his household after him”). Nowhere in Scripture, they stress, is this responsibility given to the state, church, or school. [studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/genesis-18.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/genesis-18.html)

---

## Other Views

- **Jewish tradition (cited by Ellicott, Gill, Precept Austin)**: The three visitors were three angels — Michael, Gabriel, and Raphael (Talmud, Bava Metzia 86b). Each had a single mission: one to heal Abraham from circumcision, one to announce Isaac’s birth, and one to destroy Sodom. The Targum of Jonathan renders v. 8 as “they seemed to eat,” uneasy with the idea of angels actually consuming food. [biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/18.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/18.htm); [preceptaustin.org/genesis-18-commentary](https://www.preceptaustin.org/genesis-18-commentary)

- **Catholic and Orthodox readings**: Searches to newadvent.org, catholic.com, and oca.org could not be performed within the available limits; no content from these sites was retrieved. To include those views, a further round of research would be needed.

- **Modern scholarship (NET Bible notes, cited at Precept Austin)**: The NET notes describe the passage as a theophany — “The three visitors are probably the LORD and two angels.” They observe that the drawn‑out description of Abraham’s gaze (he “lifted up his eyes and looked, and behold”) focuses the reader’s attention and signals that what he sees is significant. NET leaves open whether Abraham immediately recognised his visitors’ identity or acted “quite unwittingly.” [preceptaustin.org/genesis-18-commentary](https://www.preceptaustin.org/genesis-18-commentary)
